## From sample mean to recursive estimation

The experimental activity simulated in this post consists of acquiring a collection of $n$ measurements of some quantity at discrete instants of time that, without loss of generality, can be assumed equally spaced by an interval $\Delta T$.

The measurand, whose physical nature is irrelevant for the present discussion, is assumed for now to be constant and equal to $\mu$. Measurements are affected by additive noise modeled as a random variable $V$ with zero mean and constant variance $\sigma^2$.

The resulting measurement sequence can therefore be written as

$$
x_k=\mu+v_k,\qquad k=1,\dots,n,
$$

where the explicit time dependence has been omitted for the sake of clarity.

If measurement errors are additionally assumed independent, a basic probabilistic model consists of independent identically distributed (IID) random variables $\{X_k\}_{k=1}^n$, whose realizations are the measured values $\{x_k\}_{k=1}^n$.

So far, nothing has been assumed about the probability distribution of the measurement noise $V$.

A central result of estimation theory is that the unknown quantity $\mu$ can be estimated using the sample mean

$$
\bar X_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n X_k.
$$ {#eq-1}

The sample mean is itself a random variable with expectation

$$
\mathbb{E}[\bar X_n]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb{E}[X_k]=\mu.
$$

for every value of $n$, meaning that the estimator is unbiased.

When the random variables $X_k,\;k=1,\dots,n$ are IID, the variance of the sample mean is

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\bar X_n)=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathrm{Var}(X_k)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},
$$ {#eq-2}

showing the decrease of uncertainty as the number of measurements increases. This result ultimately relies on the fact that the variance of a sum is equal to the sum of the variances if the added terms are independent (or at least uncorrelated).

Moreover, provided that the measurement noise has finite variance, the central limit theorem implies that, for sufficiently large values of $n$, the distribution of $\bar X_n$ becomes approximately Gaussian even when the original measurement noise distribution is not.

All these results are mathematically powerful, but they also hide an important practical issue: in real experimental settings, collecting a "large" number of genuinely independent observations may be much more difficult than it first appears.

Under the additional assumption of Gaussian measurement noise,

$$
V\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),
$$

the sample mean enjoys several important optimality properties. In particular, it coincides with:

-   the least-squares (LS) solution,
-   the maximum-likelihood (ML) estimator,
-   the minimum mean-square error (MMSE) estimator.

From an LS perspective, the problem of estimating a constant measurand can also be interpreted as a particularly simple regression model. Since measurements are acquired sequentially in time, the acquisition index (or time itself) may be formally regarded as a predictor variable, while the measurements play the role of the response variable.

The key modeling assumption is that the measurand is constant. In regression terms, this corresponds to fitting an intercept-only model, or equivalently a linear model with zero slope:

$$
x_k=\beta_0+v_k.
$$

Unlike calibration problems, where constraining the slope to zero is not physically justified, here the assumption is entirely consistent with the underlying experimental model.

It is worth noting that the LS solution itself does not require Gaussian assumptions on the measurement errors. In fact, the regression coefficients are obtained simply by minimizing a quadratic cost function, which leads to a linear system of equations when its gradient is set to zero.

In ordinary linear regression, this procedure produces a straight line passing through the centroid of the observed data. In the present case, however, the slope is explicitly constrained to zero. Under this constraint, the LS solution inevitably reduces to the sample mean:

$$
\hat{\beta}_0=\bar x.
$$

Probabilistic assumptions on the measurement noise instead enter through the statistical properties and optimality properties of the estimator. In particular, under Gaussian assumptions, the sample mean is also the MMSE estimator.

Before leaving this section, an important observation can already be made: the sample mean admits a recursive formulation. If $\bar x_{k-1}$ denotes the estimate computed from the first $k-1$ observations, then the arrival of a new measurement $x_k$ produces the updated estimate

$$
\bar x_k=\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)\bar x_{k-1}+\frac{1}{k}x_k.
$$ {#eq-3}

This recursive expression is algebraically equivalent to the batch computation of the sample mean in @eq-1, but it already reveals an important idea: the estimate can be updated sequentially using the previous estimate and the newly acquired measurement. As the number of observations increases, the weight assigned to newly acquired measurements progressively decreases.

## The Kalman filter in a nutshell

When Rudolf E. Kálmán (1930--2016) introduced his recursive filtering framework in the early 1960s, the problem was not merely statistical. Modern dynamical systems — aircraft, missiles, spacecraft — were generating streams of noisy measurements that needed to be processed sequentially and in real time. Batch estimation techniques already existed, but recomputing the entire estimate from scratch whenever a new measurement became available was computationally unattractive, especially on the constrained onboard computers of that era.

Kalman's key insight was that, under linear Gaussian assumptions, the estimate could instead be updated recursively: each newly acquired measurement could be combined with the current state estimate and its uncertainty to produce an improved estimate, without storing or reprocessing the entire measurement history. Equally important, if not revolutionary, was the adoption of a state-space approach to estimation, in which the evolution of the system and the measurement process could be modeled explicitly and treated within a unified probabilistic framework.

Over the decades, Kalman's original linear framework has been extended in many directions, including nonlinear filtering approaches such as the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF), the Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF), and particle filtering methods. Despite their substantial algorithmic differences, all these approaches share the same Bayesian genealogical roots: sequentially updating probabilistic beliefs as new information becomes available.

::: callout-note
## Linear Kalman filter

In its simplest linear form, the Kalman filter (KF) can be regarded as a recursive MMSE estimator for dynamical systems observed through noise.

The KF recursively alternates between two complementary operations: a prediction step based on the dynamical model, and a correction step driven by incoming measurements, as schematically illustrated in @fig-kf-diagram.






::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Conceptual structure of the Kalman filter recursion. Model-based prediction and measurement-based correction interact continuously to update the state estimate and its uncertainty.](kf_block_diagram.png){#fig-kf-diagram}
:::
:::






For a linear discrete-time dynamical system observed through noisy measurements,

$$
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{x}_{k+1}&=\mathbf{F}_k\mathbf{x}_k+\mathbf{w}_k\\
\mathbf{z}_k&=\mathbf{H}_k\mathbf{x}_k+\mathbf{v}_k
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-4}

where the state vector is $\mathbf{x}_k\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the state transition matrix $\mathbf{F}_k$ is square $n\times n$, the measurement vector is $\mathbf{z}_k \in \mathbb{R}^m$, and $\mathbf{H}_k$ is an $m\times n$ measurement matrix.

The *process noise* $\mathbf{w}_k$ and the *measurement noise* $\mathbf{v}_k$ are Gaussian, with zero mean and specified covariance structure:

$$
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{w}_k&\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{Q}_k) \\
\mathbf{v}_k&\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{R}_k)
\end{cases}
$$

The covariance matrices $\mathbf{Q}_k$ and $\mathbf{R}_k$ reflect the assumption that the process and measurement noise components are uncorrelated across different time instants. Because the noise processes are Gaussian, uncorrelated components are also statistically independent. The matrices $\mathbf{Q}_k$ and $\mathbf{R}_k$ fully characterize the second-order statistical structure of the process and measurement noise.

In Kalman filtering notation, the symbols $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k^-$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k^+$ denote the predicted (a priori) and updated (a posteriori) state estimates at time step $k$, respectively. The corresponding estimation errors are

$$
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{e}_k^-&=\mathbf{x}_k-\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k^-\\
\mathbf{e}_k^+&=\mathbf{x}_k-\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k^+,
\end{cases}
$$

with covariance matrices

$$
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{P}_k^-&=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{e}_k^{-}(\mathbf{e}_k^{-})^\top\right] \\
\mathbf{P}_k^+&=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{e}_k^{+}(\mathbf{e}_k^{+})^\top\right].
\end{cases}
$$
:::

### Estimating the value of a constant measurand

Let us now return to the experimental scenario introduced above. The measurand is assumed constant and the measurements are affected by additive Gaussian noise. In Kalman-filter notation, this corresponds to the scalar model

$$
\begin{cases}
x_{k+1}&=x_k\\
z_k&=x_k+v_k,
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-5}

where

$$
v_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R),\qquad R=\sigma^2.
$$

We also have:

$$
F=1,\qquad H=1,\qquad Q=0.
$$

The condition $Q=0$ is particularly important. The filter is explicitly told that the state is constant: measurements are noisy, but the measurand is assumed not to evolve in time. There is therefore measurement uncertainty, but no model uncertainty associated with the state dynamics.

For the scalar model considered here, the KF equations simplify considerably. Since $F=1$ and $Q=0$, the prediction step leaves both the estimate and its uncertainty unchanged:

$$
\hat x_k^-=\hat x_{k-1}^+,\qquad P_k^-=P_{k-1}^+.
$$

The Kalman gain is therefore

$$
K_k=\frac{P_k^-}{P_k^-+R}.
$$

Suppose the filter is initialized with no prior knowledge about the value of the state. This corresponds to assigning a very large initial uncertainty to the estimate, formally $P_1^- \to \infty$. As a consequence,

$$
K_1=\frac{P_1^-}{P_1^-+R}\to 1,
$$

so the first measurement is trusted completely:

$$
\hat x_1^+=z_1.
$$

The updated covariance is

$$
P_1^+=\left(1-\frac{P_1^-}{P_1^-+R}\right)P_1^-=\frac{RP_1^-}{P_1^-+R}\to R.
$$

Because $Q=0$, the prediction step does not reinject uncertainty into the model:

$$
P_2^-=P_1^+=R.
$$

At the second iteration,

$$
K_2=\frac{R}{R+R}=\frac12.
$$

The updated estimate is therefore

$$
\hat x_2^+=\hat x_1^+ +\frac12(z_2-\hat x_1^+)=\frac{z_1+z_2}{2},
$$

and the updated covariance becomes

$$
P_2^+=\frac{R}{2}.
$$

Continuing the recursion, one obtains

$$
\hat x_k^+=\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)\hat x_{k-1}^+ +\frac{1}{k}z_k,
$$

which is exactly the formula for the sample mean introduced in @eq-3. In this special case, the Kalman gain becomes

$$
K_k=\frac{1}{k}.
$$

The KF therefore progressively stops reacting to new measurements: each additional observation receives less weight because it becomes increasingly confident that the constant quantity has already been estimated.

## Is a physical quantity ever really constant?

In the previous section, the KF state was assumed perfectly constant, corresponding to the choice $Q=0$. Let us now relax this assumption and consider the more realistic situation in which the state may slowly evolve over time.

The simplest stochastic model for a slowly varying quantity consists of describing the scalar state as a random walk driven by continuous-time white noise with strength $q$:

$$
\dot x(t) = w(t),
$$

where

$$
\mathbb{E}[w(t)w(t+\tau)] = q\,\delta(\tau).
$$

If measurements are acquired every $\Delta T$ seconds, the corresponding discrete-time model becomes

$$
x_{k+1}=x_k+\Delta w_k,
$$

where $\Delta w_k$ represents the stochastic increment accumulated over the sampling interval $\Delta T$. The variance of this discrete-time process noise is therefore

$$
Q=q\,\Delta T.
$$

This simple relation already contains an important physical idea: uncertainty accumulates over time. The longer the interval between consecutive measurements, the larger the uncertainty injected during the prediction step.

For the scalar random-walk model,

$$
\begin{cases}
x_{k+1}&=x_k+\Delta w_k \\
z_k&=x_k+v_k,
\end{cases}
$$

the KF prediction step is particularly simple. Since $F=1$ and $H=1$,

$$
P_k^-=P_{k-1}^++Q.
$$

The Kalman gain is therefore

$$
K_k=\frac{P_k^-}{P_k^-+R}=\frac{P_{k-1}^++Q}{P_{k-1}^++Q+R}.
$$

After the measurement update,

$$
P_k^+=(1-K_k)P_k^-.
$$

Substituting the expression of $K_k$,

$$
P_k^+=\left(1-\frac{P_{k-1}^++Q}{P_{k-1}^++Q+R}\right)(P_{k-1}^++Q),
$$

and therefore

$$
P_k^+=\frac{R(P_{k-1}^++Q)}{P_{k-1}^++Q+R}.
$$

This recursion is the scalar Riccati equation for the random-walk model.

The key point is what happens when the recursion reaches steady state. If

$$
P_k^+=P_{k-1}^+=P_\infty,
$$

then

$$
P_\infty=\frac{R(P_\infty+Q)}{P_\infty+Q+R}.
$$

Unlike the previous case with $Q=0$, the covariance no longer collapses toward zero because uncertainty is continuously reinjected into the model dynamics.

Solving this quadratic equation gives

$$
P_\infty=\frac{-Q+\sqrt{Q^2+4QR}}{2}.
$$

As soon as $Q>0$, the steady-state covariance remains strictly positive. Consequently, the steady-state Kalman gain is also strictly positive:

$$
K_\infty=\frac{P_\infty+Q}{P_\infty+Q+R}.
$$

The KF therefore never stops listening to new measurements.

## Simulation

The following simulation compares two KFs observing the same random-walk process. The first filter uses the correct stochastic model ($Q=q\Delta T$), where uncertainty is continuously reinjected during prediction, while the second incorrectly assumes that the state is perfectly constant ($Q=0$).






::: {.cell}

```{.matlab .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="A filter that never forgets — and one that does"}
% ********************************
% Random-walk process simulation
% ********************************

dt    = 1;          % sampling interval, s
T     = 50;         % observation time, s

q     = 1;          % continuous-time noise strength, [a.u.]^2/s
std_q = sqrt(q*dt); % discrete-time process noise std, [a.u.]
std_v = 0.1;        % measurement noise standard deviation, [a.u.]

% ***************
% Path generation
% ***************

rng(1234)

N  = T/dt + 1;
xi = zeros(N,1);

for i = 2:N
    xi(i) = xi(i-1) + sqrt(q*dt)*randn;
end

x = xi;

z_meas = x + randn(N,1)*std_v;

% ******
% Models
% ******

F = 1;
H = 1;

R = std_v^2;

Q_true = std_q^2;
Q_fake = 0;

P_0 = Q_true;

% **************
% Initialization
% **************

x_true = zeros(N, 1);
P_true = zeros(N, 1);
K_true = zeros(N, 1);

x_fake = zeros(N, 1);
P_fake = zeros(N, 1);
K_fake = zeros(N, 1);

x_pred_true = 0;
P_pred_true = P_0;

x_pred_fake = randn;
P_pred_fake = P_0;

for i = 1:N

    % *******************
    % compute Kalman gain
    % *******************

    K_true(i) = P_pred_true*H/(H*P_pred_true*H + R);
    K_fake(i) = P_pred_fake*H/(H*P_pred_fake*H + R);
  
    % ******
    % update
    % ******

    x_true(i) = x_pred_true + ...
                K_true(i)*(z_meas(i) - H*x_pred_true);

    P_true(i) = (1 - K_true(i)*H)*P_pred_true;

    x_fake(i) = x_pred_fake + ...
                K_fake(i)*(z_meas(i) - H*x_pred_fake);

    P_fake(i) = (1 - K_fake(i)*H)*P_pred_fake;

    % *************
    % project-ahead
    % *************

    x_pred_true = F*x_true(i);
    P_pred_true = F*P_true(i)*F + Q_true;

    x_pred_fake = F*x_fake(i);
    P_pred_fake = F*P_fake(i)*F + Q_fake;
    
end

% ************************
% State estimate evolution
% ************************

plot((0:N-1), x, 'k', 'LineWidth', 2)

hold on

plot((0:N-1), x_true, 'b.', ...
     (0:N-1), x_fake, 'r.', ...
     'LineWidth', 1, ...
     'MarkerSize', 18)

legend("process", ...
       "correct model", ...
       "Q = 0 model", ...
       "Location", "northwest")

xlabel('Time step')
ylabel('State [a.u.]')

set(gca, 'FontSize', 14, 'LineWidth', 2)

% ***********************
% Kalman gain evolution
% ***********************

figure

plot((0:N-1), K_true, 'b', ...
     (0:N-1), K_fake, 'r', ...
     'LineWidth', 2)

legend("correct model", ...
       "Q = 0 model")

ylim([0 1.25])

xlabel('Time step')
ylabel('Kalman gain')

set(gca, 'FontSize', 14, 'LineWidth', 2)
```
:::






@fig-kf-path compares the state estimates produced by the two KFs. While the KF using the correct process model continues to track the evolving random walk, the KF with $Q=0$ progressively loses responsiveness.






::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![State estimates produced by the two filters.](traj.png){#fig-kf-path fig-align='center' width=70%}
:::
:::






The consequences become evident in @fig-kf-gain. When $Q=0$, the Kalman gain progressively collapses toward zero and the KF gradually stops incorporating new information. By contrast, when $Q=q\Delta T$, the gain converges to a finite steady-state value, allowing the KF to remain responsive to the evolving dynamics. In other words, the KF never becomes completely certain about the system.






::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Evolution of the Kalman gain.](gain.png){#fig-kf-gain fig-align='center' width=70%}
:::
:::






To better visualize the effect of the process noise variance $Q$, the previous simulation is repeated using three different process models obtained by perturbing a nominal value of $Q$ by one order of magnitude in both directions. More precisely, the three KFs use

$$
Q=[0.1,\ 1,\ 10]\times q\Delta T,
$$

with $q=0.1$, while the measurement noise standard deviation is kept fixed at $\sigma=0.3$.

The first KF intentionally underestimates the process uncertainty and behaves as a *sleepy* filter, characterized by long memory and slow response to incoming measurements. The second KF uses the correct stochastic model and represents a balanced compromise between prediction and measurement update. The third KF largely overestimates the process uncertainty and behaves as an *awake* filter, rapidly incorporating new measurements into the state estimate.

@fig-kf-path-3q compares the resulting state estimates.






::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![State estimates obtained using different values of the process noise variance.](traj_3q.png){#fig-kf-path-3q fig-align='center' width=75%}
:::
:::






The effect of the different values of $Q$ becomes even more evident in the corresponding Kalman gains shown in @fig-kf-gain-3q.






::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Kalman gain evolution for the three filters.](gain_3q.png){#fig-kf-gain-3q fig-align='center' width=75%}
:::
:::






The process noise variance $Q$ effectively acts as a tuning knob. Small values of $Q$ produce KFs with slow response, while large values of $Q$ produce highly responsive filters that rapidly follow incoming measurements — sometimes excessively so.

This behavior is simply another manifestation of the classical trade-off between promptness of response and noise sensitivity encountered in virtually every filtering problem. In practice, mildly overestimating $Q$ is often less dangerous than underestimating it: an awake filter may become noisy, but a sleepy filter may eventually stop reacting altogether.

## Conclusion

Throughout this post, we explored how the KF adapts when the assumptions about the measurand progressively change: from a perfectly static constant ($Q=0$) to a drifting random walk with independent increments ($Q>0$). We saw how the process noise covariance $Q$ acts as a tuning knob balancing responsiveness, and noise sensitivity.

Many physical quantities, however, possess a more structured temporal behavior than a simple random walk.

In the next post, we will move one step further by modeling the measurand as a first-order Gauss–Markov process. We will see how the KF manages systems with intrinsic temporal memory — and later in this series, we will explore what happens when that memory shifts from the physical quantity itself into the sensor.
